Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line

Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line is an online encyclopedia of the anti-revisionist movements' own documents and periodicals, filed by country and by the periods of their splits and collapse, in the Marxists Internet Archive's History section; its goal is "to document this trend" (contents page; What is Anti-Revisionism, 2009; census record).

🗂️ What it holds

  • Background: a brief definition; materials from China and Albania (contents page).1↘
    Its contents open with background, "A Brief definition of Anti-Revisionism" and representative materials from China and from Albania, and file the United States by three waves of anti-revisionism from 1946 to 1970 and by the New Communist Movement from its origins in 1969 through its party-building campaigns to 1977 (contents page).§9
  • By country: 26 sections, the United States in three waves and the New Communist Movement (contents page; census record).4↘
    Its contents open with background, "A Brief definition of Anti-Revisionism" and representative materials from China and from Albania, and file the United States by three waves of anti-revisionism from 1946 to 1970 and by the New Communist Movement from its origins in 1969 through its party-building campaigns to 1977 (contents page).§9 The New Communist Movement sections that follow are titled "Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend, 1976-1977", "Crises, Splits and More New Parties, 1977-1980", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite, 1978-1980", "Collapse and Aftermath" and "Major Issues and Debates", with an alphabetical index to all its subsections (contents page).§10 Canada runs from a post-war antecedent, Fergus McKean, to "Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983", the United Kingdom from post-war antecedents through "High Tide: The Consolidation of Maoism by the Late 1970’s" to "Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution", and 23 further countries from Australia to Switzerland have a section each (contents page), 26 country sections by the census's count, document counts not stated (maryleelabor census record).§11 The census record takes as its unit "a primary document of an anti-revisionist movement, organization or party, filed by country and by period subsection; periodicals listed by country", and as what it records 26 countries with China and Albania, the United States from 1946 to the New Communist Movement's collapse, Canada 1964 to 1983 and the United Kingdom to "decline and dissolution" (maryleelabor census record).§12
  • By its splits: "Crises, Splits and More New Parties", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite", "Collapse and Aftermath"; Canada's collapse; Britain's "Ebbing Tide" (contents page).3↘
    The New Communist Movement sections that follow are titled "Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend, 1976-1977", "Crises, Splits and More New Parties, 1977-1980", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite, 1978-1980", "Collapse and Aftermath" and "Major Issues and Debates", with an alphabetical index to all its subsections (contents page).§10 Canada runs from a post-war antecedent, Fergus McKean, to "Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983", the United Kingdom from post-war antecedents through "High Tide: The Consolidation of Maoism by the Late 1970’s" to "Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution", and 23 further countries from Australia to Switzerland have a section each (contents page), 26 country sections by the census's count, document counts not stated (maryleelabor census record).§11 Its losing side, in the census record, is its structure: "the encyclopedia is organized around splits and defeat", shown by the United States, Canadian and British section titles (maryleelabor census record).§13
  • Periodicals: by country, some named by their splits, running to 2011 (periodicals page).4↘
    Its periodicals page lists the movements' papers and journals by country, among them The African World, Challenge/Desafio, the Progressive Labor Party's newspaper, Revolutionary Worker and Workers’ Advocate (1969-93) in the United States, The Forge and In Struggle in Canada and Proletarian in Britain (periodicals page), the list the census record counts among its holdings (maryleelabor census record).§14 It names periodicals by the splits that made them: the Chicago Workers’ Voice of "former members of the Marxist-Leninist Party", and the Young Communist "after it went with the Revolutionary Workers Headquarters in the RCP split" (periodicals page).§15 Its list runs past 1983, to Eureka (2000-2005), Demarcations ("starting in 2009") and The Line of March ("begun 2011") (periodicals page), where the census record gives the period from 1946 "to the 1980s", records movements that "ended or dissolved by its own section titles" and tags it "NOT a living movement's site" (maryleelabor census record).§16 #1725 draws its SDS case from a document in EROL's New Communist Movement section, the REP collective's account of the 1969 expulsion of Progressive Labor, calls the SDS record "the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down", and concludes "The split took the place of the discussion" (#1725); Challenge/Desafio, the newspaper of the party expelled, stands on the encyclopedia's periodicals page (periodicals page).§27

📉 The trend

  • The term: opposition to revising revolutionary fundamentals; a post-war trend in the pro-Soviet movement (2009 page).1↘
    The trend, on the same page, is first the term's older use, "opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals of revolutionary theory and practice in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries", and in its specific meaning "a trend that developed in the pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist) Communist movement after World War II" (What is Anti-Revisionism, Paul C., 2009).§6
  • Its course: 1956, the defence of Stalin, Chinese and Albanian alignments, the Sino-Soviet split, decline after Mao (2009 page).2↘
    It grew at the shift from wartime collaboration to the Cold War and at the crisis of the CPSU's 20th Congress in 1956, criticized the official Communist Parties "from the left" for abandoning orthodox Marxism-Leninism and for being insufficiently revolutionary, and made the defence of Stalin its hallmark once those parties joined Khrushchev's denunciation of him (What is Anti-Revisionism).§7 It expanded to communists aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions, reached its greatest size with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution and declined after Mao's death and the defeat of the Gang of Four, when some "soldiered on" and others argued for a non-Trotskyist "left-wing" communism independent of foreign authorities or models (What is Anti-Revisionism); the census record adds that "The tendency it records is itself a minority defined against 'revisionism'" (maryleelabor census record).§8
  • A minority: "defined against 'revisionism'" (census record).1↘
    It expanded to communists aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions, reached its greatest size with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution and declined after Mao's death and the defeat of the Gang of Four, when some "soldiered on" and others argued for a non-Trotskyist "left-wing" communism independent of foreign authorities or models (What is Anti-Revisionism); the census record adds that "The tendency it records is itself a minority defined against 'revisionism'" (maryleelabor census record).§8

🧭 Whose record

  • Kept: the movements' documents "in the encyclopedia's own periodization" (census record).1↘
    The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, an area whose definition includes "the record of splits", and the texts of the tradition, with movement documents, periodical runs and primary texts as its evidence, and answers that it keeps "the anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties: their primary documents and periodicals, in the encyclopedia's own periodization", which tells "how the encyclopedia periodizes a national movement's waves, splits and collapse" (maryleelabor census record).§22
  • Reading: "An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record"; "the losing side of the losing side" (census record).1↘
    The archive's reading in the record is "An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record in that tendency's own documents, sectioned by its splits and its collapse, so each faction of a split stays stated after the organization that housed it ended"; it reads the "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite" and "Major Issues and Debates" sections "as the losing side of the losing side kept for later readers, held by an archive independent of every party it records", and tags it "NOT an organ of any party it records" (maryleelabor census record).§23
  • Organ, holder, route: what a defeated critique keeps if it is to be taken up later (#1725).3↘
    The census names #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes, as its anchor (maryleelabor census record); #1725 holds that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender", and that otherwise "the defeated critique loses its organ, its holder and its route, and so cannot be taken up later" (#1725).§24 #1725 states the conventional reading first, in which "the New Communist Movement's succession of parties" looks like proof and "the left's problem is temperamental: too much fighting", and reads the record by its endings: "Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending", a critique being "settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows" or leaving "with the people who hold it" (#1725).§25 Where a dispute concerns the group's identity, #1725 holds, "a split is the honest outcome, and the question becomes whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and where a critique was later taken up its critics "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper" (#1725).§26
  • SDS: #1725's record of the 1969 expulsion is a document EROL holds, "the winning side wrote it down"; the expelled party's paper is listed too (#1725; periodicals page).2↘
    Its periodicals page lists the movements' papers and journals by country, among them The African World, Challenge/Desafio, the Progressive Labor Party's newspaper, Revolutionary Worker and Workers’ Advocate (1969-93) in the United States, The Forge and In Struggle in Canada and Proletarian in Britain (periodicals page), the list the census record counts among its holdings (maryleelabor census record).§14 #1725 draws its SDS case from a document in EROL's New Communist Movement section, the REP collective's account of the 1969 expulsion of Progressive Labor, calls the SDS record "the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down", and concludes "The split took the place of the discussion" (#1725); Challenge/Desafio, the newspaper of the party expelled, stands on the encyclopedia's periodicals page (periodicals page).§27

🔒 Holder and terms

  • Holder: an EROL Administrator, under the MIA; terms unstated (contents page; census record).2↘
    It is entered from the Marxists Internet Archive's History section, "MIA: History: Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line" (entry page), its contents page ends "Contact EROL Administrator" (contents page), and Harvard's record gives the Marxists Internet Archive as its creator and its parent source (Harvard Digital Handbook).§3 The census record has it held by "an EROL Administrator, under the Marxists Internet Archive", with "terms are not stated on the saved EROL pages", and records it as part of that archive by its URL, the relation unstated in prose on the contents page (maryleelabor census record).§4
  • Host: volunteer, non-profit, politically independent; public domain unless noted (MIA introduction; Wikipedia).2↘
    The host gives itself as "an all-volunteer, non-profit public library, established in its present form in 1998", with 76 active volunteers in July 2025, bound by the tenets "We will always remain politically independent", "We do not ‘judge’ writers" and "Our priority is to provide archival information", endorsing none of the views of the writers it archives (MIA introduction, last updated 21 April 2026).§17 Its licence is the host's, "All material within these Archives, unless noted otherwise, is public domain" (MIA introduction), which the census record carries for EROL beside "not stated on the saved EROL pages", with access by "free public web pages" (maryleelabor census record); the Wikipedia article on the host says its collection is maintained by volunteers and its material free of charge, "although not necessarily free of copyright" (Wikipedia).§18
  • Harvard's limit: "has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy" (Harvard Digital Handbook).3↘
    Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a "Digital encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, containing English translations of representative anti-Revisionist materials from China, Albania, and many western countries", in the format "Digital archive", item OARRSH_00098 of its Open Access Primary Sources (Harvard Digital Handbook).§2 Harvard's record dates its materials "1946-1983", lists 26 places of coverage from the USSR, China and Albania to Switzerland, without India, Iran or the Philippines, and gives its subjects as anti-Revisionism, the Sino-Soviet split, foreign relations, the Cold War and ideology, its language English (Harvard Digital Handbook).§19 The same record states a limit: "This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy", for it "may reproduce copyright-protected content without license or permissions, contain re-typed content that cannot be verified for accuracy or completeness, and/or omit facts of publication or archival attribution" (Harvard Digital Handbook).§20
  • Unstated: limits, gathering method, completeness, the administrator (census record).1↘
    The census record states no limits of the saved pages ("not stated on the saved pages"), notes that the gathering method "is not described on the saved page", does not answer "the completeness of its holdings for any organization" or "the record of tendencies outside anti-revisionism", and leaves unchecked "who the EROL Administrator is, and how documents were gathered", its introduction page having returned HTTP 404 (maryleelabor census record).§21

📋 Reception

  • Wikipedia: a redirect to the Marxists Internet Archive, whose article does not name it (Wikipedia).2↘
    The Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line, EROL in the census record, states its holding in its own heading as "INFORMATION ON AND PRIMARY DOCUMENTS FROM ANTI-REVISIONIST MOVEMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND PARTIES BY COUNTRY" (contents page), and the maryleelabor census enters it as an "online encyclopedia of information on, and primary documents from, anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties, by country" (maryleelabor census record).§1 The English Wikipedia has no article on it: the name redirects to "Marxists Internet Archive", whose article defines the host as "a non-profit online encyclopedia, created in 1990" and names its historical sections and a reference section, the "Encyclopedia of Marxism", without naming EROL (Wikipedia), which the census record tags "NOT a general encyclopedia of Marxism" (maryleelabor census record).§28
  • At the name: subject and range held; the splits "not in the composition" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).2↘
    At its name the Overview carries the encyclopedia's "Definition, period, countries and periodicals", "Faithful to the encyclopedia's subject and range", with "The MIA named as its host", at a new address, the census name, for an external resource entered in the census the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§29 The Capture Registry records "THE SPLITS NOT CARRIED", "The composition gives the movement as a country entry", and "its periodization by splits, unity attempts and collapse, is not in the composition", and attributes to #1725 a reading of "EROL as a record kept of a movement's failure to hold its own critiques, organized by that failure" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); #1725 names omission "the expulsion form: the contested record never reaches the answer-forming context" (#1725).§30
  • Period: Harvard dates it 1946-1983, the census to the 1980s; the periodicals run to 2011 (Harvard; census record; periodicals page).2↘
    Its list runs past 1983, to Eureka (2000-2005), Demarcations ("starting in 2009") and The Line of March ("begun 2011") (periodicals page), where the census record gives the period from 1946 "to the 1980s", records movements that "ended or dissolved by its own section titles" and tags it "NOT a living movement's site" (maryleelabor census record).§16 Harvard's record dates its materials "1946-1983", lists 26 places of coverage from the USSR, China and Albania to Switzerland, without India, Iran or the Philippines, and gives its subjects as anti-Revisionism, the Sino-Soviet split, foreign relations, the Cold War and ideology, its language English (Harvard Digital Handbook).§19

[QUERENT] Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line

[SYSTEM] The [Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVWhgc2mPY5qa5nKPfGI6Tc2yFNBp2l2w-o9GcPIdg-o8U3ogYj55BJuPCfFJWKBo2-YGNkMYA5WgCWszZQPBHDJNXLAEvkxMyf3hWpB4Bk6xXBpvXSDYIhI_C3xwo_xYaSQ) (EROL) is a digital archive developed by the Marxists Internet Archive containing primary source documents, translations, and organizational records from the international anti-revisionist and Marxist-Leninist/Maoist movements. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVWhgc2mPY5qa5nKPfGI6Tc2yFNBp2l2w-o9GcPIdg-o8U3ogYj55BJuPCfFJWKBo2-YGNkMYA5WgCWszZQPBHDJNXLAEvkxMyf3hWpB4Bk6xXBpvXSDYIhI_C3xwo_xYaSQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAVTOrmDZ9ykPWsBNby1RL-SowmVKydeZ_PSuXsk4VJdRIBOaE49nLwue8w56zcO3MO7HbXAqK1XR0T6j2GaSOORECO2eUI3o7mI0KKnvFi4Zy0yMMXZIVny56AFHXOCSxUtPmgNV-QvN9B55bI6WHzLU4EDDQ9)]
Core Definition

* Anti-Revisionism: Opposition to abandoning orthodox revolutionary theory. It arose as a post-WWII critique of official communist parties—particularly following the Soviet Union's de-Stalinization under Nikita Khrushchev in 1956—which anti-revisionists viewed as insufficiently revolutionary. Groups later split to align with either Chinese or Albanian political and ideological positions during the Sino-Soviet split. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAV8LmGxI7xaAiuNuq_s9crAvwEZbVg19X3gvo6kALf5EwTM1oP_9tJQEngD6S6-cn9VV80yNXjswbRyh06c6bhXTVqhlYtIfm-cDwovwePMg8nYlqioOJD0WZPQ0JBXHsEmA), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVWhgc2mPY5qa5nKPfGI6Tc2yFNBp2l2w-o9GcPIdg-o8U3ogYj55BJuPCfFJWKBo2-YGNkMYA5WgCWszZQPBHDJNXLAEvkxMyf3hWpB4Bk6xXBpvXSDYIhI_C3xwo_xYaSQ)]

Scope and Contents

* Timeframe: Primarily covers materials spanning roughly 1946 to 1983, growing significantly during the Sino-Soviet split and the Chinese Cultural Revolution. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVWhgc2mPY5qa5nKPfGI6Tc2yFNBp2l2w-o9GcPIdg-o8U3ogYj55BJuPCfFJWKBo2-YGNkMYA5WgCWszZQPBHDJNXLAEvkxMyf3hWpB4Bk6xXBpvXSDYIhI_C3xwo_xYaSQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAV8LmGxI7xaAiuNuq_s9crAvwEZbVg19X3gvo6kALf5EwTM1oP_9tJQEngD6S6-cn9VV80yNXjswbRyh06c6bhXTVqhlYtIfm-cDwovwePMg8nYlqioOJD0WZPQ0JBXHsEmA), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAVTOrmDZ9ykPWsBNby1RL-SowmVKydeZ_PSuXsk4VJdRIBOaE49nLwue8w56zcO3MO7HbXAqK1XR0T6j2GaSOORECO2eUI3o7mI0KKnvFi4Zy0yMMXZIVny56AFHXOCSxUtPmgNV-QvN9B55bI6WHzLU4EDDQ9)]
* Geographic Coverage: Includes documentation, background materials, and party histories from:
   * North America: United States (first to third waves, New Communist Movement) and Canada (post-WWII antecedents and waves).
   * Europe: United Kingdom, Albania, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Italy, Norway, Denmark, Ireland, Iceland, Belgium, Switzerland.
   * Asia & Oceania: China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Philippines, Australia, New Zealand.
   * Latin America & Africa: Chile, Nicaragua, Eritrea, Ethiopia. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVWhgc2mPY5qa5nKPfGI6Tc2yFNBp2l2w-o9GcPIdg-o8U3ogYj55BJuPCfFJWKBo2-YGNkMYA5WgCWszZQPBHDJNXLAEvkxMyf3hWpB4Bk6xXBpvXSDYIhI_C3xwo_xYaSQ)]
* Periodicals & Publications: The archive indexes historical newspapers, bulletins, and theoretical journals from various groups (such as Challenge/Desafio and Workers' Advocate in the U.S., The Forge and In Struggle in Canada, and Proletarian in the UK). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScwHrOzAV0P_nhP93d-rrOCaejYZifK8YWfDlapo_2ynBCXyCe8Ta2FYkkndENRuWEn4ZB_W1AylGS2nCqhtI2SmQU7qQdzVQGF3qzDhRTy9zy11RSQ7yXrhna4WpnC1BAfpnE3fU-7itiMtlYKCW2dPZVkQ)]

Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line

The Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line, EROL in the census record, states its holding in its own heading as "INFORMATION ON AND PRIMARY DOCUMENTS FROM ANTI-REVISIONIST MOVEMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND PARTIES BY COUNTRY" (contents page), and the maryleelabor census enters it as an "online encyclopedia of information on, and primary documents from, anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties, by country" (maryleelabor census record). Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a "Digital encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, containing English translations of representative anti-Revisionist materials from China, Albania, and many western countries", in the format "Digital archive", item OARRSH_00098 of its Open Access Primary Sources (Harvard Digital Handbook). It is entered from the Marxists Internet Archive's History section, "MIA: History: Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line" (entry page), its contents page ends "Contact EROL Administrator" (contents page), and Harvard's record gives the Marxists Internet Archive as its creator and its parent source (Harvard Digital Handbook). The census record has it held by "an EROL Administrator, under the Marxists Internet Archive", with "terms are not stated on the saved EROL pages", and records it as part of that archive by its URL, the relation unstated in prose on the contents page (maryleelabor census record). Its definition page closes on its purpose: "The goal of the Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism is to document this trend", signed "Paul C., 2009" (What is Anti-Revisionism).

The trend, on the same page, is first the term's older use, "opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals of revolutionary theory and practice in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries", and in its specific meaning "a trend that developed in the pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist) Communist movement after World War II" (What is Anti-Revisionism, Paul C., 2009). It grew at the shift from wartime collaboration to the Cold War and at the crisis of the CPSU's 20th Congress in 1956, criticized the official Communist Parties "from the left" for abandoning orthodox Marxism-Leninism and for being insufficiently revolutionary, and made the defence of Stalin its hallmark once those parties joined Khrushchev's denunciation of him (What is Anti-Revisionism). It expanded to communists aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions, reached its greatest size with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution and declined after Mao's death and the defeat of the Gang of Four, when some "soldiered on" and others argued for a non-Trotskyist "left-wing" communism independent of foreign authorities or models (What is Anti-Revisionism); the census record adds that "The tendency it records is itself a minority defined against 'revisionism'" (maryleelabor census record).

Its contents open with background, "A Brief definition of Anti-Revisionism" and representative materials from China and from Albania, and file the United States by three waves of anti-revisionism from 1946 to 1970 and by the New Communist Movement from its origins in 1969 through its party-building campaigns to 1977 (contents page). The New Communist Movement sections that follow are titled "Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend, 1976-1977", "Crises, Splits and More New Parties, 1977-1980", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite, 1978-1980", "Collapse and Aftermath" and "Major Issues and Debates", with an alphabetical index to all its subsections (contents page). Canada runs from a post-war antecedent, Fergus McKean, to "Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983", the United Kingdom from post-war antecedents through "High Tide: The Consolidation of Maoism by the Late 1970’s" to "Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution", and 23 further countries from Australia to Switzerland have a section each (contents page), 26 country sections by the census's count, document counts not stated (maryleelabor census record). The census record takes as its unit "a primary document of an anti-revisionist movement, organization or party, filed by country and by period subsection; periodicals listed by country", and as what it records 26 countries with China and Albania, the United States from 1946 to the New Communist Movement's collapse, Canada 1964 to 1983 and the United Kingdom to "decline and dissolution" (maryleelabor census record). Its losing side, in the census record, is its structure: "the encyclopedia is organized around splits and defeat", shown by the United States, Canadian and British section titles (maryleelabor census record).

Its periodicals page lists the movements' papers and journals by country, among them The African World, Challenge/Desafio, the Progressive Labor Party's newspaper, Revolutionary Worker and Workers’ Advocate (1969-93) in the United States, The Forge and In Struggle in Canada and Proletarian in Britain (periodicals page), the list the census record counts among its holdings (maryleelabor census record). It names periodicals by the splits that made them: the Chicago Workers’ Voice of "former members of the Marxist-Leninist Party", and the Young Communist "after it went with the Revolutionary Workers Headquarters in the RCP split" (periodicals page). Its list runs past 1983, to Eureka (2000-2005), Demarcations ("starting in 2009") and The Line of March ("begun 2011") (periodicals page), where the census record gives the period from 1946 "to the 1980s", records movements that "ended or dissolved by its own section titles" and tags it "NOT a living movement's site" (maryleelabor census record).

The host gives itself as "an all-volunteer, non-profit public library, established in its present form in 1998", with 76 active volunteers in July 2025, bound by the tenets "We will always remain politically independent", "We do not ‘judge’ writers" and "Our priority is to provide archival information", endorsing none of the views of the writers it archives (MIA introduction, last updated 21 April 2026). Its licence is the host's, "All material within these Archives, unless noted otherwise, is public domain" (MIA introduction), which the census record carries for EROL beside "not stated on the saved EROL pages", with access by "free public web pages" (maryleelabor census record); the Wikipedia article on the host says its collection is maintained by volunteers and its material free of charge, "although not necessarily free of copyright" (Wikipedia). Harvard's record dates its materials "1946-1983", lists 26 places of coverage from the USSR, China and Albania to Switzerland, without India, Iran or the Philippines, and gives its subjects as anti-Revisionism, the Sino-Soviet split, foreign relations, the Cold War and ideology, its language English (Harvard Digital Handbook). The same record states a limit: "This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy", for it "may reproduce copyright-protected content without license or permissions, contain re-typed content that cannot be verified for accuracy or completeness, and/or omit facts of publication or archival attribution" (Harvard Digital Handbook). The census record states no limits of the saved pages ("not stated on the saved pages"), notes that the gathering method "is not described on the saved page", does not answer "the completeness of its holdings for any organization" or "the record of tendencies outside anti-revisionism", and leaves unchecked "who the EROL Administrator is, and how documents were gathered", its introduction page having returned HTTP 404 (maryleelabor census record).

The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, an area whose definition includes "the record of splits", and the texts of the tradition, with movement documents, periodical runs and primary texts as its evidence, and answers that it keeps "the anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties: their primary documents and periodicals, in the encyclopedia's own periodization", which tells "how the encyclopedia periodizes a national movement's waves, splits and collapse" (maryleelabor census record). The archive's reading in the record is "An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record in that tendency's own documents, sectioned by its splits and its collapse, so each faction of a split stays stated after the organization that housed it ended"; it reads the "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite" and "Major Issues and Debates" sections "as the losing side of the losing side kept for later readers, held by an archive independent of every party it records", and tags it "NOT an organ of any party it records" (maryleelabor census record). The census names #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes, as its anchor (maryleelabor census record); #1725 holds that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender", and that otherwise "the defeated critique loses its organ, its holder and its route, and so cannot be taken up later" (#1725). #1725 states the conventional reading first, in which "the New Communist Movement's succession of parties" looks like proof and "the left's problem is temperamental: too much fighting", and reads the record by its endings: "Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending", a critique being "settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows" or leaving "with the people who hold it" (#1725). Where a dispute concerns the group's identity, #1725 holds, "a split is the honest outcome, and the question becomes whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and where a critique was later taken up its critics "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper" (#1725). #1725 draws its SDS case from a document in EROL's New Communist Movement section, the REP collective's account of the 1969 expulsion of Progressive Labor, calls the SDS record "the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down", and concludes "The split took the place of the discussion" (#1725); Challenge/Desafio, the newspaper of the party expelled, stands on the encyclopedia's periodicals page (periodicals page).

The English Wikipedia has no article on it: the name redirects to "Marxists Internet Archive", whose article defines the host as "a non-profit online encyclopedia, created in 1990" and names its historical sections and a reference section, the "Encyclopedia of Marxism", without naming EROL (Wikipedia), which the census record tags "NOT a general encyclopedia of Marxism" (maryleelabor census record). At its name the Overview carries the encyclopedia's "Definition, period, countries and periodicals", "Faithful to the encyclopedia's subject and range", with "The MIA named as its host", at a new address, the census name, for an external resource entered in the census the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The Capture Registry records "THE SPLITS NOT CARRIED", "The composition gives the movement as a country entry", and "its periodization by splits, unity attempts and collapse, is not in the composition", and attributes to #1725 a reading of "EROL as a record kept of a movement's failure to hold its own critiques, organized by that failure" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); #1725 names omission "the expulsion form: the contested record never reaches the answer-forming context" (#1725).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line

Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line is an online encyclopedia of primary documents from anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties by country, in the Marxists Internet Archive's History section, its goal "to document this trend" (contents page; What is Anti-Revisionism, 2009).

🗂️ What it holds

  • Background: a definition; China and Albania (contents page).1↘
    The contents give background on the term and materials from China and Albania, then the United States in three waves from 1946 and the New Communist Movement from 1969, with an index (contents page).§5
  • By country: 26 sections; the United States in waves and the New Communist Movement (contents page).2↘
    The contents give background on the term and materials from China and Albania, then the United States in three waves from 1946 and the New Communist Movement from 1969, with an index (contents page).§5 Canada runs to crisis and collapse in 1982-1983, the United Kingdom to decline and dissolution, and 23 further countries have sections, with a periodicals list and an EROL Administrator as contact (contents page).§7
  • Splits and collapse: section titles for the NCM, Canada and Britain (contents page).2↘
    The later New Communist Movement sections are titled by the anti-dogmatist trend, crises and splits, the anti-dogmatists' failure to unite, collapse and aftermath, and major debates (contents page).§6 Canada runs to crisis and collapse in 1982-1983, the United Kingdom to decline and dissolution, and 23 further countries have sections, with a periodicals list and an EROL Administrator as contact (contents page).§7
  • Periodicals: by country, to 2011 (periodicals page).1↘
    The periodicals page lists papers and journals by country, Challenge/Desafio, Revolutionary Worker, Workers’ Advocate, The Forge, In Struggle and Proletarian among them, names some by the splits that produced them, and runs to periodicals begun in 2009 and 2011 (periodicals page).§8

📉 The trend

  • Term: opposition to revising fundamentals; a post-war pro-Soviet trend (2009 page).1↘
    Its definition page, signed Paul C., 2009, sets as its goal documenting the anti-revisionist trend, in the term's older sense of opposition to revising revolutionary fundamentals and its specific sense of a post-war trend in the pro-Soviet, non-Trotskyist Communist movement (What is Anti-Revisionism).§2
  • Course: 1956, Stalin, China and Albania, decline after Mao (2009 page).2↘
    The trend grew with the Cold War and the crisis of 1956, criticized the official parties from the left, defended Stalin after Khrushchev's denunciation, and expanded to Chinese and Albanian alignments (What is Anti-Revisionism).§3 It peaked with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution, declined after Mao's death, and divided between those who adapted and those who sought a left-wing communism independent of foreign models (What is Anti-Revisionism).§4

🔒 Holder and terms

  • Holder: an EROL Administrator; the MIA as creator (contents page; Harvard).2↘
    Canada runs to crisis and collapse in 1982-1983, the United Kingdom to decline and dissolution, and 23 further countries have sections, with a periodicals list and an EROL Administrator as contact (contents page).§7 Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a digital encyclopedia and archive developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, with English translations of materials from China, Albania and many western countries, dated 1946-1983 (Harvard Digital Handbook).§9
  • Catalogue: 1946-1983; English translations (Harvard).1↘
    Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a digital encyclopedia and archive developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, with English translations of materials from China, Albania and many western countries, dated 1946-1983 (Harvard Digital Handbook).§9
  • Limit: not found to meet all criteria for legitimacy (Harvard).1↘
    Harvard's record warns that it has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy and may reproduce copyright-protected or unverifiable re-typed content (Harvard Digital Handbook).§10
  • Host: volunteer, non-profit, independent; public domain unless noted (MIA introduction).2↘
    Its host describes itself as an all-volunteer, non-profit public library in its present form since 1998, politically independent, endorsing none of the views it archives, with material public domain unless noted otherwise (MIA introduction).§11 Wikipedia has no article on the encyclopedia; the name redirects to the Marxists Internet Archive, a volunteer-maintained online encyclopedia created in 1990 whose material is not necessarily free of copyright, and whose article does not name EROL (Wikipedia).§12
  • Wikipedia: a redirect to the host's article (Wikipedia).1↘
    Wikipedia has no article on the encyclopedia; the name redirects to the Marxists Internet Archive, a volunteer-maintained online encyclopedia created in 1990 whose material is not necessarily free of copyright, and whose article does not name EROL (Wikipedia).§12

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)12 sentences · every one sourced below

Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line

The Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line, entered from the History section of the Marxists Internet Archive, gives information on and primary documents from anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties by country (entry page; contents page). Its definition page, signed Paul C., 2009, sets as its goal documenting the anti-revisionist trend, in the term's older sense of opposition to revising revolutionary fundamentals and its specific sense of a post-war trend in the pro-Soviet, non-Trotskyist Communist movement (What is Anti-Revisionism). The trend grew with the Cold War and the crisis of 1956, criticized the official parties from the left, defended Stalin after Khrushchev's denunciation, and expanded to Chinese and Albanian alignments (What is Anti-Revisionism). It peaked with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution, declined after Mao's death, and divided between those who adapted and those who sought a left-wing communism independent of foreign models (What is Anti-Revisionism).

The contents give background on the term and materials from China and Albania, then the United States in three waves from 1946 and the New Communist Movement from 1969, with an index (contents page). The later New Communist Movement sections are titled by the anti-dogmatist trend, crises and splits, the anti-dogmatists' failure to unite, collapse and aftermath, and major debates (contents page). Canada runs to crisis and collapse in 1982-1983, the United Kingdom to decline and dissolution, and 23 further countries have sections, with a periodicals list and an EROL Administrator as contact (contents page). The periodicals page lists papers and journals by country, Challenge/Desafio, Revolutionary Worker, Workers’ Advocate, The Forge, In Struggle and Proletarian among them, names some by the splits that produced them, and runs to periodicals begun in 2009 and 2011 (periodicals page).

Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a digital encyclopedia and archive developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, with English translations of materials from China, Albania and many western countries, dated 1946-1983 (Harvard Digital Handbook). Harvard's record warns that it has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy and may reproduce copyright-protected or unverifiable re-typed content (Harvard Digital Handbook). Its host describes itself as an all-volunteer, non-profit public library in its present form since 1998, politically independent, endorsing none of the views it archives, with material public domain unless noted otherwise (MIA introduction). Wikipedia has no article on the encyclopedia; the name redirects to the Marxists Internet Archive, a volunteer-maintained online encyclopedia created in 1990 whose material is not necessarily free of copyright, and whose article does not name EROL (Wikipedia).

register entry encyclopedia-of-anti-revisionism-on-line-aio-20261031 OBS-34ab72c3b78b · file as first run sha256 412f461987fe5fbf…

  • T1-1 definition: 'The Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line (EROL) is a digital archive developed by the Marxists Internet Archive containing primary source documents, translations, and organizational records from the international anti-revisionist and Marxist-Leninist/Maoist movements.' (two markers)
  • T1-2 core definition: 'Anti-Revisionism: Opposition to abandoning orthodox revolutionary theory. It arose as a post-WWII critique of official communist parties—particularly following the Soviet Union's de-Stalinization under Nikita Khrushchev in 1956—which anti-revisionists viewed as insufficiently revolutionary. Groups later split to align with either Chinese or Albanian political and ideological positions during the Sino-Soviet split.' (two markers)
  • T1-3 timeframe: 'Primarily covers materials spanning roughly 1946 to 1983, growing significantly during the Sino-Soviet split and the Chinese Cultural Revolution.' (three markers)
  • T1-4 geographic coverage: 'Includes documentation, background materials, and party histories from:' North America (the United States 'first to third waves, New Communist Movement'; Canada 'post-WWII antecedents and waves'), Europe (13, Albania among them), Asia & Oceania (9, China among them), Latin America & Africa (4) (one marker)
  • T1-5 periodicals: 'The archive indexes historical newspapers, bulletins, and theoretical journals from various groups (such as Challenge/Desafio and Workers' Advocate in the U.S., The Forge and In Struggle in Canada, and Proletarian in the UK).' (one marker)
  • T1-6 pointer (closer): 'You can browse the full collection, regional documents, and foundational essays directly via the Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line Index and read an overview of the ideology at What is Anti-Revisionism.' (two markers)

E_A, the archive's entity: the same encyclopedia, in the maryleelabor census record and the archive's deposits: an online encyclopedia of anti-revisionist movement documents by country, in the areas of movement documents and the texts of the tradition, whose unit is a primary document filed by country and period subsection; keeping the movements' documents and periodicals in its own periodization; held by an EROL Administrator under the Marxists Internet Archive on terms unstated; its losing side its structure, organized around splits and defeat, its tendency a minority defined against revisionism; read by the archive as an organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record, sectioned by its splits, held independently of every party it records; measured against the anchor's conditions for a defeated critique to be taken up later (an organ, a holder, a route) and its question whether a split is recorded and argued or enacted; one of its documents the anchor's record of the 1969 SDS expulsion, written by the winning side; whose composition at its own name leaves its periodization by splits out (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31) ML-01 ML-05 ML-08 ML-10 ML-11 ML-12 ML-14 ML-24 ML-25 ML-35 O1725-06 O1725-07 D1725-01 CAP-1-07; defining papers #1725

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: an online encyclopedia and document archive of the anti-revisionist movements, a section of the Marxists Internet Archive)): the online encyclopedia served at www.marxists.org/history/erol/, entered from the Marxists Internet Archive's History section, giving information on and primary documents from anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties by country (contents page), its goal 'to document this trend' (Paul C., 2009), anti-revisionism being a post-war trend in the pro-Soviet Communist movement that grew after 1956 and the Sino-Soviet split and declined after Mao (definition page); its contents a background section with materials from China and Albania, the United States in three waves and the New Communist Movement through its splits, collapse and debates, Canada to its collapse in 1982-1983, Britain to its decline and dissolution and 23 further countries, with a periodicals list by country running to 2011 and an EROL Administrator as contact; catalogued by Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History as a digital encyclopedia developed by the MIA with English translations, dated 1946-1983, with the limit that it has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy; its host an all-volunteer, non-profit, politically independent public library whose material is public domain unless noted; with no Wikipedia article, its name a redirect to the host's article

ρ = extends: The archive reads the Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line as its own pages present it and adds, on the field's own object: the census's question of whose record it keeps, who holds it and whether it keeps the losing side; its losing side read as its structure, its sections of splits and collapse; the archive's reading of it as an organ of a defeated tendency's record, independent of every party it records; the anchor's conditions under which a defeated critique can be taken up later, and its use of one of the encyclopedia's documents as the winning side's record of a split; what the census leaves unchecked (the administrator, the gathering, completeness); and the composition layer's omission, at its name, of its periodization by splits. ML-35 ML-10 ML-12 ML-24 ML-25 O1725-06 O1725-07 D1725-01 ML-33 CAP-1-07. Guard: ρ = extends claims an addition and no more (§1.2a). It does not make the field's sources wrong at their dates. Where an archive claim stands against a field claim (ML-17, ML-28 and ML-31, the period to the 1980s and the movements ended, against F34, periodicals dated 2000-2011; ML-27, the public-domain licence, against F28 and F44), both are composed under P_coh within the one ontology, and ML-24 is composed beside D1725-01 within the archive. The archive's class claims (#1725) are claims on the classes the field and the census source for the entity (anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties; archives of movement and party documents), never on the entity by the composer's judgment.

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The maryleelabor census record describes the Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line from its own pages, each field with its basis on the contents page or the host's introduction, and answers for it the census's question of whose record it keeps, who holds it and whether it keeps the losing side; its one reading of its own, ml_reading, takes the encyclopedia's section titles (the field's F5, F7, F8) as an organ of the defeated tendency's record. #1725, the census's anchor, gives the terms of that question (organ, holder, route; the ending of a dispute; the split recorded and argued or enacted) and draws one case from a document the encyclopedia holds; it does not contest what the encyclopedia is. The capture record checks the composition against the encyclopedia's pages. No defining source contests the field's ontology of the entity or supplies one the field lacks: the archive adds the question of the record, its losing side and its holder, on the field's own object.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology424 words

The Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line, entered from the History section of the Marxists Internet Archive, gives information on and primary documents from anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties by country (entry page; contents page). Its definition page, signed Paul C., 2009, sets as its goal documenting the anti-revisionist trend, in the term's older sense of opposition to revising revolutionary fundamentals and its specific sense of a post-war trend in the pro-Soviet, non-Trotskyist Communist movement (What is Anti-Revisionism). The trend grew with the Cold War and the crisis of 1956, criticized the official parties from the left, defended Stalin after Khrushchev's denunciation, and expanded to Chinese and Albanian alignments (What is Anti-Revisionism). It peaked with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution, declined after Mao's death, and divided between those who adapted and those who sought a left-wing communism independent of foreign models (What is Anti-Revisionism). The contents give background on the term and materials from China and Albania, then the United States in three waves from 1946 and the New Communist Movement from 1969, with an index (contents page). The later New Communist Movement sections are titled by the anti-dogmatist trend, crises and splits, the anti-dogmatists' failure to unite, collapse and aftermath, and major debates (contents page). Canada runs to crisis and collapse in 1982-1983, the United Kingdom to decline and dissolution, and 23 further countries have sections, with a periodicals list and an EROL Administrator as contact (contents page). The periodicals page lists papers and journals by country, Challenge/Desafio, Revolutionary Worker, Workers’ Advocate, The Forge, In Struggle and Proletarian among them, names some by the splits that produced them, and runs to periodicals begun in 2009 and 2011 (periodicals page). Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a digital encyclopedia and archive developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, with English translations of materials from China, Albania and many western countries, dated 1946-1983 (Harvard Digital Handbook). Harvard's record warns that it has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy and may reproduce copyright-protected or unverifiable re-typed content (Harvard Digital Handbook). Its host describes itself as an all-volunteer, non-profit public library in its present form since 1998, politically independent, endorsing none of the views it archives, with material public domain unless noted otherwise (MIA introduction). Wikipedia has no article on the encyclopedia; the name redirects to the Marxists Internet Archive, a volunteer-maintained online encyclopedia created in 1990 whose material is not necessarily free of copyright, and whose article does not name EROL (Wikipedia).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1789 words

The Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line, EROL in the census record, states its holding in its own heading as "INFORMATION ON AND PRIMARY DOCUMENTS FROM ANTI-REVISIONIST MOVEMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND PARTIES BY COUNTRY" (contents page), and the maryleelabor census enters it as an "online encyclopedia of information on, and primary documents from, anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties, by country" (maryleelabor census record). Harvard's Digital Handbook for Research on Soviet History catalogues it as a "Digital encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, containing English translations of representative anti-Revisionist materials from China, Albania, and many western countries", in the format "Digital archive", item OARRSH_00098 of its Open Access Primary Sources (Harvard Digital Handbook). It is entered from the Marxists Internet Archive's History section, "MIA: History: Encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism On-Line" (entry page), its contents page ends "Contact EROL Administrator" (contents page), and Harvard's record gives the Marxists Internet Archive as its creator and its parent source (Harvard Digital Handbook). The census record has it held by "an EROL Administrator, under the Marxists Internet Archive", with "terms are not stated on the saved EROL pages", and records it as part of that archive by its URL, the relation unstated in prose on the contents page (maryleelabor census record). Its definition page closes on its purpose: "The goal of the Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism is to document this trend", signed "Paul C., 2009" (What is Anti-Revisionism). The trend, on the same page, is first the term's older use, "opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals of revolutionary theory and practice in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries", and in its specific meaning "a trend that developed in the pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist) Communist movement after World War II" (What is Anti-Revisionism, Paul C., 2009). It grew at the shift from wartime collaboration to the Cold War and at the crisis of the CPSU's 20th Congress in 1956, criticized the official Communist Parties "from the left" for abandoning orthodox Marxism-Leninism and for being insufficiently revolutionary, and made the defence of Stalin its hallmark once those parties joined Khrushchev's denunciation of him (What is Anti-Revisionism). It expanded to communists aligned with Chinese or Albanian positions, reached its greatest size with Marxist-Leninist and Maoist parties after the Sino-Soviet split, grew with the Cultural Revolution and declined after Mao's death and the defeat of the Gang of Four, when some "soldiered on" and others argued for a non-Trotskyist "left-wing" communism independent of foreign authorities or models (What is Anti-Revisionism); the census record adds that "The tendency it records is itself a minority defined against 'revisionism'" (maryleelabor census record). Its contents open with background, "A Brief definition of Anti-Revisionism" and representative materials from China and from Albania, and file the United States by three waves of anti-revisionism from 1946 to 1970 and by the New Communist Movement from its origins in 1969 through its party-building campaigns to 1977 (contents page). The New Communist Movement sections that follow are titled "Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend, 1976-1977", "Crises, Splits and More New Parties, 1977-1980", "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite, 1978-1980", "Collapse and Aftermath" and "Major Issues and Debates", with an alphabetical index to all its subsections (contents page). Canada runs from a post-war antecedent, Fergus McKean, to "Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983", the United Kingdom from post-war antecedents through "High Tide: The Consolidation of Maoism by the Late 1970’s" to "Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution", and 23 further countries from Australia to Switzerland have a section each (contents page), 26 country sections by the census's count, document counts not stated (maryleelabor census record). The census record takes as its unit "a primary document of an anti-revisionist movement, organization or party, filed by country and by period subsection; periodicals listed by country", and as what it records 26 countries with China and Albania, the United States from 1946 to the New Communist Movement's collapse, Canada 1964 to 1983 and the United Kingdom to "decline and dissolution" (maryleelabor census record). Its losing side, in the census record, is its structure: "the encyclopedia is organized around splits and defeat", shown by the United States, Canadian and British section titles (maryleelabor census record). Its periodicals page lists the movements' papers and journals by country, among them The African World, Challenge/Desafio, the Progressive Labor Party's newspaper, Revolutionary Worker and Workers’ Advocate (1969-93) in the United States, The Forge and In Struggle in Canada and Proletarian in Britain (periodicals page), the list the census record counts among its holdings (maryleelabor census record). It names periodicals by the splits that made them: the Chicago Workers’ Voice of "former members of the Marxist-Leninist Party", and the Young Communist "after it went with the Revolutionary Workers Headquarters in the RCP split" (periodicals page). Its list runs past 1983, to Eureka (2000-2005), Demarcations ("starting in 2009") and The Line of March ("begun 2011") (periodicals page), where the census record gives the period from 1946 "to the 1980s", records movements that "ended or dissolved by its own section titles" and tags it "NOT a living movement's site" (maryleelabor census record). The host gives itself as "an all-volunteer, non-profit public library, established in its present form in 1998", with 76 active volunteers in July 2025, bound by the tenets "We will always remain politically independent", "We do not ‘judge’ writers" and "Our priority is to provide archival information", endorsing none of the views of the writers it archives (MIA introduction, last updated 21 April 2026). Its licence is the host's, "All material within these Archives, unless noted otherwise, is public domain" (MIA introduction), which the census record carries for EROL beside "not stated on the saved EROL pages", with access by "free public web pages" (maryleelabor census record); the Wikipedia article on the host says its collection is maintained by volunteers and its material free of charge, "although not necessarily free of copyright" (Wikipedia). Harvard's record dates its materials "1946-1983", lists 26 places of coverage from the USSR, China and Albania to Switzerland, without India, Iran or the Philippines, and gives its subjects as anti-Revisionism, the Sino-Soviet split, foreign relations, the Cold War and ideology, its language English (Harvard Digital Handbook). The same record states a limit: "This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy", for it "may reproduce copyright-protected content without license or permissions, contain re-typed content that cannot be verified for accuracy or completeness, and/or omit facts of publication or archival attribution" (Harvard Digital Handbook). The census record states no limits of the saved pages ("not stated on the saved pages"), notes that the gathering method "is not described on the saved page", does not answer "the completeness of its holdings for any organization" or "the record of tendencies outside anti-revisionism", and leaves unchecked "who the EROL Administrator is, and how documents were gathered", its introduction page having returned HTTP 404 (maryleelabor census record). The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, an area whose definition includes "the record of splits", and the texts of the tradition, with movement documents, periodical runs and primary texts as its evidence, and answers that it keeps "the anti-revisionist movements, organizations and parties: their primary documents and periodicals, in the encyclopedia's own periodization", which tells "how the encyclopedia periodizes a national movement's waves, splits and collapse" (maryleelabor census record). The archive's reading in the record is "An organ that keeps a defeated tendency's record in that tendency's own documents, sectioned by its splits and its collapse, so each faction of a split stays stated after the organization that housed it ended"; it reads the "Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite" and "Major Issues and Debates" sections "as the losing side of the losing side kept for later readers, held by an archive independent of every party it records", and tags it "NOT an organ of any party it records" (maryleelabor census record). The census names #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes, as its anchor (maryleelabor census record); #1725 holds that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender", and that otherwise "the defeated critique loses its organ, its holder and its route, and so cannot be taken up later" (#1725). #1725 states the conventional reading first, in which "the New Communist Movement's succession of parties" looks like proof and "the left's problem is temperamental: too much fighting", and reads the record by its endings: "Disagreement is constant. What varies is the ending", a critique being "settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows" or leaving "with the people who hold it" (#1725). Where a dispute concerns the group's identity, #1725 holds, "a split is the honest outcome, and the question becomes whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and where a critique was later taken up its critics "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper" (#1725). #1725 draws its SDS case from a document in EROL's New Communist Movement section, the REP collective's account of the 1969 expulsion of Progressive Labor, calls the SDS record "the clearest single instance, because the winning side wrote it down", and concludes "The split took the place of the discussion" (#1725); Challenge/Desafio, the newspaper of the party expelled, stands on the encyclopedia's periodicals page (periodicals page). The English Wikipedia has no article on it: the name redirects to "Marxists Internet Archive", whose article defines the host as "a non-profit online encyclopedia, created in 1990" and names its historical sections and a reference section, the "Encyclopedia of Marxism", without naming EROL (Wikipedia), which the census record tags "NOT a general encyclopedia of Marxism" (maryleelabor census record). At its name the Overview carries the encyclopedia's "Definition, period, countries and periodicals", "Faithful to the encyclopedia's subject and range", with "The MIA named as its host", at a new address, the census name, for an external resource entered in the census the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The Capture Registry records "THE SPLITS NOT CARRIED", "The composition gives the movement as a country entry", and "its periodization by splits, unity attempts and collapse, is not in the composition", and attributes to #1725 a reading of "EROL as a record kept of a movement's failure to hold its own critiques, organized by that failure" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); #1725 names omission "the expulsion form: the contested record never reaches the answer-forming context" (#1725).

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): At 'Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism On-Line' (T1, five cards: B1–B5, all fetched; 238 words, 11 markers, a closing pointer to the index and the definition page) the composition gives the encyclopedia, its host, the trend it records, its period, its countries and its periodicals. Composed from its cards, at their grain or coarser: the definition at the grain of Harvard's catalogue record (B4 F22: 'Digital encyclopedia of anti-Revisionism developed by the Marxists Internet Archive, containing English translations'; F27 'Digital archive'; F23 the MIA as creator), with the contents page's 'PRIMARY DOCUMENTS FROM ANTI-REVISIONIST MOVEMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND PARTIES' (B1 F1) as 'primary source documents … and organizational records'; the trend from the definition page (B2 F11–F14, F16–F18) through card 2's snippet, whose words 'Opposition to abandoning orthodox revolutionary theory' T carries and which summarize F11 and are no span of the page; the period 1946 to 1983 (B4 F24, the contents page's sections running 1946-1950 to 1982-1983, F3, F7); the countries (B1 F2, F3, F4, F9; B4 F25), all 26 sections with China and Albania placed among the countries as Harvard's coverage places them; the periodicals (B5 F30–F33: Challenge/Desafio, Workers’ Advocate, The Forge, In Struggle, Proletarian). Available in the field and left out of the composition (§6.2, 'available, not composed'): the encyclopedia's own statement of purpose, 'The goal of the Encyclopedia of Anti-Revisionism is to document this trend', and its signature 'Paul C., 2009' (B2 F20); the New Communist Movement's later sections, 'Birth of the Anti-Dogmatist Trend', 'Crises, Splits and More New Parties', 'Anti-Dogmatists Unable to Unite', 'Collapse and Aftermath', 'Major Issues and Debates' (B1 F5), Canada's 'Crisis and Collapse, 1982-1983' (F7) and Britain's 'High Tide' and 'Ebbing Tide: Decline and Dissolution' (F8), which T composes as 'United States (first to third waves, New Communist Movement)', 'Canada (post-WWII antecedents and waves)' and a bare 'United Kingdom'; the contact 'EROL Administrator' (F10); the entry page's placement in the MIA's History section (B3 F21); the defence of Stalin as the trend's hallmark (B2 F15); the decline after Mao and the turn to an independent left-wing communism (F18's second clause, F19); Harvard's subjects and source types (F26) and its collection (F29); the periodicals named by their splits (B5 F35) and those dated after 1983 (F34). Limit dropped: Harvard's own limit on the card T draws its definition and date from, 'This online resource has not been found to meet all criteria for legitimacy' (B4 F28); T composes the record's attribution and dates and leaves its warning out. Limit dropped also on F11: the older sense is 'opposition to attempts to revise, modify or abandon the fundamentals … in a manner that was perceived to represent concessions to Communism’s adversaries'; T1-2's 'Opposition to abandoning orthodox revolutionary theory' drops 'perceived' and the adversaries clause, and composes the term's historical usage as its definition. Force raised: none observed at the period; T1-3's 'Primarily covers materials spanning roughly 1946 to 1983' hedges Harvard's catalogue date (F24), and the periodicals page, card 5, lists entries dated 1969-93, 2000-2005, 'starting in 2009' and 'begun 2011' (F31, F34), which T leaves out. Substituted reading: T1-2's 'Groups later split to align with either Chinese or Albanian political and ideological positions' composes as a split what the definition page states as expansion, 'expanded and diversified to encompass those communists who rejected a pro-Soviet orientation for one aligned either with Chinese or Albanian positions' (F16); T1-3's 'growing significantly during the Sino-Soviet split and the Chinese Cultural Revolution' attaches to the collection's materials the growth the definition page states of the trend (F17, F18). T1-2 drops F12's 'pro-Soviet (as opposed to the Trotskyist)', which card 2's snippet carries ('pro-Soviet'). Composed without attribution: the definition of the trend, at the definition page's grain, with markers and no name; coarse, common-knowledge grain, recorded. The operator attribution 'developed by the Marxists Internet Archive' is Harvard's (F22), carried as a fact with markers. Outside the cards: 'party histories', 'foundational essays', 'regional documents' (no field claim states them); 'translations' is Harvard's 'English translations' (F22). Not surfaced, admitted to B by the operator's ruling: the host's introduction (B6: an 'all-volunteer, non-profit public library', politically independent, endorsing no writer's views, its material 'public domain' unless noted, F36–F41) and Wikipedia (B8: the name a redirect to the host's article, which does not name the encyclopedia, F42–F45). Of the cards' 35 claims, T composes 21 at their grain or coarser.

v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity (an online encyclopedia of anti-revisionist documents, hosted by the MIA). T composes the encyclopedia as a catalogue entry would, at Harvard's grain: host, translations, period, countries, periodicals. It leaves out what the encyclopedia's own pages say of its organization and purpose: the sections titled by the movements' splits and collapse, the signed statement of its goal, the administrator; and it leaves out the limit Harvard sets beside the description it takes. Its period is the catalogue's, and its 'split' is its own word for the trend's expansion.

Held under P_coh within the one ontology: the census's period ('to the 1980s', ML-17), lifecycle (ML-28) and tag 'NOT a living movement's site' (ML-31) beside the periodicals dated 2000-2011 (F34); the census's licence (ML-27) beside Harvard's limit (F28) and Wikipedia's 'not necessarily free of copyright' (F44); the census's reading of the encyclopedia as keeping the defeated tendency's own documents (ML-24) beside #1725's use of it for the winning side's account (D1725-01). Not surfaced: every archive source; no card cites the census record (CAP-1-12: the record entered the census the same day).
